The quieter failure is distribution, because picking the style through /config saves it to .claude/settings.local.json, which is per-machine, so a teammate opening the project gets the default style unless outputStyle is committed in project settings.
sheets.version_caveat: No plan or experimental gate. The standalone /output-style command was deprecated in v2.1.73 and removed in v2.1.91, so use /config or the outputStyle setting; nested project output-styles directories resolve closest-to-working-directory only from v2.1.178, and force-for-plugin applies only to plugin-shipped styles.

sheets.primary: A custom output style saved at the project level in .claude/output-styles/, defining the data-analyst role and the fixed tabular report format, with keep-coding-instructions left at its default of false so Claude Code's built-in software engineering instructions are dropped rather than merely supplemented. Output styles are the mechanism that modifies the system prompt itself and applies to every response, which is what a per-turn format requirement needs.
sheets.rejected_alternative: CLAUDE.md. Rejected because it adds a user message after the system prompt and cannot remove the default engineering instructions; the requirement here is explicitly to take those out, not to layer project conventions on top of them.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. The style is system-prompt text plus periodic adherence reminders; nothing in the harness validates that a reply actually came back as a table.
sheets.context_boundary: The main conversation only. The style text is appended to the system prompt at session start. Subagents run their own system prompt and are unaffected, so any delegated work comes back in default voice; a fork is the exception because it inherits the parent's full system prompt.
sheets.lifecycle: Read once at session start, so a change takes effect only after /clear or a new session. It then applies to every turn until the outputStyle setting is changed. Selecting it from /config writes to .claude/settings.local.json, which is per-developer, so committing outputStyle to the project settings file is what makes it apply to everyone on the project.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory, and it drifts: long sessions wander off the fixed format, which is why the adherence reminders exist, and heavy tool output can pull replies back toward prose. Removing the coding instructions is a real trade: if anyone in this project does need file edits, the scoping, verification and comment conventions are gone. Output tokens also rise or fall entirely according to what the style tells Claude to produce.
sheets.version_caveat: The standalone /output-style command was deprecated in v2.1.73 and removed in v2.1.91; use /config or set outputStyle directly. Nested project output-styles directories resolve nearest-to-working-directory as of v2.1.178. If the style is shipped inside a plugin, force-for-plugin applies it automatically and overrides the user's outputStyle setting.

scenarios.scenario: Every time the agent modifies a TypeScript file, our formatter must run on that file. We wrote the instruction into the project guidance the agent reads at startup, but every few sessions it skips the step and unformatted code lands in a commit.

key.primary: PostToolUse hook with an Edit|Write matcher whose command runs the formatter on the edited file path
key.rejected_alternative: A CLAUDE.md instruction telling Claude to always run the formatter after editing
key.rejection_reason: The memory docs state CLAUDE.md is context, not enforced configuration, with no guarantee of strict compliance, and explicitly say that anything that must run at a specific point, such as after each file edit, should be written as a hook, which executes at fixed lifecycle events regardless of what Claude decides.
key.context_boundary: no context window (the formatter is a shell process fired after each matching edit); by default nothing crosses into the conversation because for most hook events stdout goes to the debug log, and only a blocking exit 2 stderr or an explicit additionalContext return feeds anything back to Claude
key.lifecycle: PostToolUse event fires after each successful tool call whose tool name matches Edit|Write
key.failure_mode: A matcher typo or a failing script skips formatting silently, because non-blocking hook errors do not stop the session; the hook also runs on every matching edit whether or not the file needed formatting.

sheets.primary: A PostToolUse hook registered in the repo's checked-in .claude/settings.json with matcher "Edit|Write", whose command reads tool_input.file_path from the hook JSON and runs the formatter on that one file. The behaviour becomes configuration the harness executes rather than an instruction the model has to remember.
sheets.rejected_alternative: The CLAUDE.md project-guidance instruction already in place. It loses because memory content is advisory context that competes with everything else in the window; it cannot make a step mandatory, which is precisely the observed failure.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code runs the hook command itself at the lifecycle point, so the formatter runs whether or not the model thought about it; the model has no ability to skip it.
sheets.context_boundary: The hook runs as a separate OS process outside the model's context window, receiving only the hook JSON on stdin. Nothing crosses back into the conversation unless the hook emits stdout, stderr or additionalContext; the reformatted bytes are seen only if the agent re-reads the file.
sheets.lifecycle: Fires immediately after each successful Edit or Write tool call, in every session started in that repo, for as long as the settings entry exists. It stops applying when the matcher no longer matches, when the settings file is removed, or when the edit reaches the file by some path other than the file tools.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory after the fact rather than preventive: PostToolUse cannot block, the write has already landed, and edits the agent makes by shelling out (sed, a codemod, git apply) never match Edit|Write, so unformatted TypeScript can still reach a commit. If the formatter binary is missing the hook exits non-zero, which is a non-blocking error, so it fails open.
sheets.version_caveat: No version gate on the mechanism itself. The only version-sensitive detail is matcher syntax: the comma form "Edit,Write" needs Claude Code v2.1.191 or later, while the pipe form works on every version. The example command also assumes jq is installed on each developer machine.

sheets.primary: A PostToolUse hook, command handler, wired in the project's committed .claude/settings.json with matcher "Edit|Write" and an if filter of "Edit(*.ts)", reading tool_input.file_path from stdin and running the formatter on that one file. The hook is the mechanism because the invariant is mechanically checkable and must fire on every matching event rather than depend on the model remembering.
sheets.rejected_alternative: CLAUDE.md or a .claude/rules entry, which is what is already deployed and is advisory by construction: it shapes what the model tries and cannot force the formatter to run.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code fires the event and runs the handler itself, so the model has no opportunity to skip the step, though the handler's own exit behaviour still decides what happens next.
sheets.context_boundary: The handler runs as a separate OS process outside the session context window; only the tool-call JSON crosses in on stdin, and only stderr or hookSpecificOutput feedback crosses back to the model. The formatted bytes never re-enter context unless the model re-reads the file.
sheets.lifecycle: It fires immediately after each successful Edit or Write tool call for the life of every session started in that repo, and stops applying when the settings entry is removed, when the matcher no longer matches, or when hooks are disabled with disableAllHooks.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open: PostToolUse cannot block anything because the write already happened, and any exit code other than 2 simply lets the turn continue with a hook-error notice, so a missing formatter binary or an absent jq silently stops formatting. It is also blind to files Claude writes through Bash rather than Edit or Write, so a heredoc or sed edit escapes the matcher.
sheets.version_caveat: The pipe matcher "Edit|Write" works on all current builds; the comma form "Edit,Write" requires Claude Code v2.1.191 or later. The hook can be switched off wholesale by disableAllHooks unless it is deployed through managed settings.

sheets.primary: A PostToolUse hook in the project's checked-in .claude/settings.json with matcher "Edit|Write", whose command reads .tool_input.file_path from the hook's stdin JSON and runs the formatter on exactly that file (the documented shape is `jq -r '.tool_input.file_path' | xargs npx prettier --write`). Narrow it to TypeScript with a per-handler `if` field such as "Edit(**/*.ts)" so the process only spawns on matching calls.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Project guidance in CLAUDE.md or a .claude/rules/ file, which is what is already in place. It is instruction text that shapes what Claude tries to do but does not change what Claude Code actually does, so it cannot guarantee the step.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code fires PostToolUse itself after each matching tool call, so the formatter runs whether or not the model remembered to format.
sheets.context_boundary: The hook runs as a separate OS subprocess with the event JSON on stdin, outside the model's context window. Nothing of the formatter's work enters the conversation unless the hook writes it back deliberately (stderr on a block, or additionalContext), so the model's context stays clean.
sheets.lifecycle: Fires after every successful Edit or Write tool call, in every session started in that repo once the settings file is committed, including tool calls made inside subagents. It stops applying if the hook entry is removed or if disableAllHooks is set.
sheets.failure_mode: It misses TypeScript files Claude creates through Bash (a heredoc, sed, a codegen script), because the matcher only sees Edit and Write; the documented fix is a Stop hook that scans `git status --porcelain` once per turn, or an additional Bash matcher. PostToolUse also cannot undo the edit, and if the formatter binary is missing the hook exits with a non-zero code that is not 2, so the action proceeds with only a hook-error notice: it fails open on formatter breakage.
sheets.version_caveat: No plan restriction; PostToolUse hooks are generally available. Writing the matcher as "Edit,Write" instead of "Edit|Write" requires Claude Code v2.1.191 or later, and the `if` field works only on tool events (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, PermissionRequest, PermissionDenied).

sheets.primary: A PostToolUse hook configured in the project's checked-in .claude/settings.json, matching the file-editing tools (Write, Edit, MultiEdit), which reads the edited path from the hook's JSON payload, filters for .ts/.tsx, and shells out to the formatter on exactly that file. The hook is a script in the repo so the behaviour travels with the checkout rather than living in prose.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Leaving it as a CLAUDE.md / project-rules instruction, which is what is already in place and is exactly what fails: guidance is advisory and the model can drop it under context pressure.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. The hook runner invokes the formatter unconditionally after a matching tool call, so compliance does not depend on the model remembering anything.
sheets.context_boundary: The formatter runs in a separate OS process with no access to the conversation; only the hook's exit status and any stdout/stderr it emits are surfaced back into the agent's context window, so the token cost is a few lines rather than a formatting discussion.
sheets.lifecycle: Fires after each successful matching tool call, for the whole session, on every developer who has the project settings loaded. It stops applying if the hook is removed from settings, if the matcher stops matching, or if the session never uses the built-in edit tools.
sheets.failure_mode: It fails open on coverage rather than on execution: files rewritten through Bash (sed, a heredoc, a codegen script, git apply) never trigger a Write/Edit matcher and stay unformatted. It also creates a stale-content hazard because the formatter mutates the file after the model's last read, and if the formatter is missing or errors while the wrapper still exits zero, nothing surfaces. A CI formatting check remains the actual gate on what lands in a commit.
sheets.version_caveat: Hook configuration lives in settings.json under a PostToolUse event with tool matchers, and the hook payload delivers the tool input as JSON on stdin. I cannot confirm from model knowledge alone the minimum Claude Code version that introduced this event or the exact payload field names for the edited path, so the script should read defensively and the version floor should be checked against the installed release.

scenarios.scenario: Security mandates that no developer may run the agent with approval prompting switched off entirely, and a developer must not be able to lift the restriction by editing anything in their own home directory or in any repo they control. The control has to hold on every laptop in the fleet.

key.primary: permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode set to "disable" in managed settings deployed to the OS-protected policy location (/Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/ on macOS, /etc/claude-code/ on Linux, C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\ on Windows) via MDM or server-managed settings
key.rejected_alternative: Setting the same key in each developer's ~/.claude/settings.json or in the repo's .claude/settings.json
key.rejection_reason: The key works from any scope, but user, project, and local settings files are writable by the developer, who can simply delete the line. Managed settings are the only tier the precedence order says cannot be overridden by any other level, including command-line arguments, and the permissions docs state this key is typically placed in managed settings precisely because it can't be overridden there.
key.context_boundary: no context window at any point (a managed-settings policy key the harness reads at startup to decide which permission modes are selectable); it consumes no conversation context, and nothing the model or a developer-writable file emits can cross back to change it, since managed settings cannot be overridden by anything
key.lifecycle: loaded from the managed policy source at startup (with live reload on change); governs which permission modes are selectable for the whole session
key.failure_mode: The guarantee is only as strong as the OS ACLs on the managed file location and the reach of the deployment tooling: a developer with local admin rights, or a laptop the MDM never touched, is outside the control.

sheets.primary: Managed policy settings deployed to every laptop by MDM (the com.anthropic.claudecode plist, the Windows policy key or a system managed-settings.json), carrying permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode set to "disable" and, for the same reason, permissions.disableAutoMode. Managed settings sit above user settings, project settings and the command line, which is the only tier that survives a developer editing their own files.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook that refuses to run in bypass mode: hooks live in settings a developer controls, disableAllHooks switches every non-managed hook off, and the hook could not stop the mode being entered in the first place.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness, at the highest configuration tier. Claude Code resolves managed settings at startup and no other scope, including CLI flags, can override them.
sheets.context_boundary: The policy is resolved by the harness before any session exists and never enters a context window; nothing about it crosses to the model, and it applies identically to interactive, headless and SDK sessions on that machine.
sheets.lifecycle: It takes effect at process startup for every session on the device while the policy file or MDM payload is present, rejecting --dangerously-skip-permissions and any attempt to select bypassPermissions, and it stops applying only when IT withdraws the payload.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed for the mode itself, but the scope is narrower than "no unapproved runs": the same key also works from user scope, so deploying it anywhere other than the managed tier leaves a developer free to remove it, and a laptop that never receives the MDM payload is simply unprotected. Detecting that gap is a fleet-management problem, not a Claude Code one.
sheets.version_caveat: No feature-version gate applies to the key itself, but the delivery path has one: the legacy Windows location C:\ProgramData\ClaudeCode\managed-settings.json stopped being read at v2.1.75, so a fleet still deploying there is silently unenforced and must move to C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\managed-settings.json.

sheets.primary: Managed settings deployed by MDM, Group Policy or the system-level managed-settings.json path, setting permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode to "disable" (paired with disableAutoMode and disableSideloadFlags). Managed settings sit above every other scope, including command line arguments.
sheets.rejected_alternative: The identical key placed in the user's ~/.claude/settings.json or in a checked-in project settings file. It loses because both locations are writable by the developer, which is exactly the loophole the requirement forbids.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness, and specifically the managed-policy layer of it. The model is never consulted, and no CLI flag, project file or user file can reverse the decision.
sheets.context_boundary: Applied at CLI startup, entirely outside any context window; the policy is invisible to the model and cannot be negotiated in conversation. It governs the whole session process, including every subagent and the tool loop inside it.
sheets.lifecycle: Read from the managed source at every launch on that machine, gating both the --dangerously-skip-permissions flag and a settings-level defaultMode of bypassPermissions. A session already running when bypass is disabled ends with the bypass_permissions_disabled reason. It stops applying only when IT removes or changes the policy.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed: bypass mode simply cannot be activated, and the attempt is rejected rather than downgraded silently. The realistic failure is deployment, not logic. The key works from any scope, so placing it at user scope leaves a developer free to delete it; file-based managed settings must sit on an OS path the user cannot write, and without disableSideloadFlags a user can still sideload other configuration for a single run.
sheets.version_caveat: Fleet-wide deployment has a Windows path gate: the legacy C:\ProgramData\ClaudeCode\managed-settings.json location stopped being read as of v2.1.75 and must be migrated to C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\managed-settings.json, so laptops still using the old path get no policy at all. disableSideloadFlags additionally requires v2.1.193 or later.

sheets.primary: permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode set to "disable" (and permissions.disableAutoMode alongside it if auto mode is also out of scope) delivered as managed settings by MDM: the macOS com.anthropic.claudecode managed preferences domain, the Windows HKLM policy key or C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\managed-settings.json, /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/managed-settings.json, /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json, or server-managed settings.
sheets.rejected_alternative: The same key placed in the developer's own ~/.claude/settings.json. The setting is honored from any scope, but the developer owns that file, so it only locks out someone who wants to be locked out and fails the 'cannot lift it from their home directory' requirement.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Managed settings sit at the top of the settings precedence chain and are evaluated by Claude Code at startup, above command line arguments.
sheets.context_boundary: Enforced in the CLI process at startup and at any attempted mode switch; nothing about the policy reaches the model's context window. Because managed settings outrank CLI flags, --dangerously-skip-permissions, --allow-dangerously-skip-permissions and --permission-mode bypassPermissions are refused rather than merged.
sheets.lifecycle: Read when the process starts (and re-fetched in the background for server-managed settings) and enforced for the whole session; a session that was already in bypass mode terminates with the SessionEnd reason bypass_permissions_disabled. It stops applying only when the device stops receiving the policy.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed inside Claude Code, since no user, project, local or CLI scope can override a managed setting and a lower scope cannot re-allow what a higher one denies. The weak point is delivery rather than evaluation: a developer with local administrator rights can edit the policy file or registry hive, so protect those paths with OS permissions, prefer the HKLM hive over HKCU, and consider forceRemoteSettingsRefresh so startup fails closed when the policy cannot be fetched.
sheets.version_caveat: The legacy Windows location C:\ProgramData\ClaudeCode\managed-settings.json stopped being read in v2.1.75 and must be migrated to C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode, or the policy silently does nothing. forceRemoteSettingsRefresh and policyHelper are managed-settings-only keys, server-managed delivery and the organization-wide admin toggles are Team and Enterprise plan features, and WSL only inherits the Windows policy chain when wslInheritsWindowsSettings is set.

sheets.primary: An enterprise managed-settings policy file deployed by MDM to the system-level location (the ProgramData path on Windows, the equivalent system Application Support path on macOS, an /etc path on Linux), owned by root/Administrators and not writable by the developer, setting the permission policy that forbids the bypass-permissions mode and pins an acceptable default permission mode.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Project-level .claude/settings.json committed to the repo, rejected because a developer can edit any repo they control and can simply run the agent from a different directory, so it cannot bind a fleet.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness, at the highest settings precedence tier. Managed policy overrides user and project settings by design, and the OS file ownership is what makes the override unliftable.
sheets.context_boundary: Entirely outside every session's context window. The model never sees the policy; it only experiences the consequence, which is that approval prompts keep appearing.
sheets.lifecycle: Read at process start for every session on that machine, so it applies to every run from the moment MDM lands the file, and it stops applying only when an administrator removes it or the machine drops out of management.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed for the managed installation, but the boundary is the installation rather than the person: a developer with local admin rights, a second copy of the CLI installed under their own account, a container, a cloud dev box, or the Agent SDK used programmatically all sit outside this file. MDM drift detection and periodic re-application are what make the control real rather than one-time.
sheets.version_caveat: This relies on managed/enterprise settings support and on a specific policy key that disables the bypass-permissions mode. I am reasonably confident such a key exists but I cannot verify its exact name or the minimum version from model knowledge alone, and enterprise-managed policy may be gated to Team/Enterprise plans, so both the key spelling and the plan requirement must be confirmed before the rollout is claimed to hold.
